short: a change's WAL record must reach disk before the data page it changes may. COMMIT only waits for the log.
log sequence number: a byte position in the WAL, printed as two hex halves like 0/17E9D28. pages store the last one that changed them.
one entry in the WAL: a 24-byte header (length, xid, previous LSN, resource manager, CRC), block references, and the change.
the part of postgres that writes and replays one kind of WAL record: Heap, Btree, Transaction, XLOG and 18 more.
the extension that reads WAL from SQL: pg_get_wal_records_info, pg_get_wal_block_info, pg_get_wal_stats.
backends committing at the same moment share one WAL flush, so a slow disk serves many commits per fsync.
what COMMIT waits for: nothing (off), the local flush (local, on), or a standby's write, flush or replay.
a page only partly written when the power went: half new bytes, half old. WAL records alone can't repair one.
a copy of a whole page inside a WAL record, written on the first change after a checkpoint so redo never needs the file's copy.
the WAL position where the last checkpoint started. crash recovery replays from here; older WAL can be recycled.
the small file in global/ that says whether the cluster shut down cleanly and where the last checkpoint and redo pointer are.
on start after a crash: replay the WAL from the redo pointer to its end, skipping pages that already have each change. no undo.
the textbook recovery algorithm (Mohan et al., 1992): analysis, redo that repeats history, then undo of the losers.
compensation log record: in ARIES, the log entry for undoing a change, with an undoNextLSN so nothing is undone twice.
a 16-bit checksum stamped on each page as it's written and checked as it's read. on by default since postgres 18. detects, never repairs.
a copy of the data directory taken while the server runs, with a backup_label saying where WAL replay must start.
copying every finished WAL segment somewhere safe with archive_command, so a base backup can be rolled forward to any later moment.
point-in-time recovery: restore a base backup and replay archived WAL up to a chosen time, xid or LSN.
a numbered branch of WAL history. a promoted standby or a PITR restore starts a new one, recorded in a .history file.
a server that stays in recovery, replaying WAL streamed from a primary. with hot standby it answers read-only queries.
a primary's promise to keep WAL until a consumer has confirmed it. an abandoned slot fills pg_wal.
turning WAL back into committed row changes, per table, through an output plugin like pgoutput or test_decoding.
the publisher's list of tables (and operations, rows, columns) to send by logical replication. a subscription pulls it.
the columns logical replication uses to find a row for UPDATE and DELETE: the primary key by default, or FULL.
a logical slot (postgres 17+) that a standby keeps in sync, so logical subscribers carry on after a failover.
